items.body:
One of the UK’s most distinctive filmmakers returns to the sea, replete with his original synth score - as on ‘Bait’ and ‘Enys Men’ - but notably damper, deeply blue; surely evoking fellow Cornish native AFX’s ‘SAW II’, BoC interludes, Mordant Music, classic folk horror OSTs.

Centred around the tale of a trawler that returns, sans crew, to a Cornish harbour years after it was thought lost, ‘The Rose Of Nevada’ typically draws on what Mark Jenkin knows best - the people, places and metaphysics of the Atlantic peninsula - whilst ideally emphasising the atmosphere with his special ingredient score. His palette of tape-smudged analog synths feels especially washed out and suggestive of his subject in its briny tone and oceanic scale, which evidently works a treat as a discrete work in its own right, severed from imagery. 

There’s possibly a Kernewek word for “hiraeth”, or “sehnsucht” - a sense of longing, nostalgia - that we’re not aware of, but may perfectly fit the feeling of Jenkin’s music here. Sea-legged loops and sustained drones colour the air with a palpable melancholy in passage from the bittersweet tang of ‘Kneebone Barton’, as used on the trailer, and throughout the album’s patches of decaying wheeze, staining the surface like rust or efflorescence on weathered coves. 

And in the day-dreamiest sense it all fades in/out of consciousness with a perfectly ghostly wow and flutter, as leaching from ‘Through The Gaps’ parts into the slurred whorl of ‘What’s Your Name,’ ephemeral concrète of ‘Look At It’, and final folksy shuffle off into the horizon with ‘Rose of Nevada.’ Here’s looking forward to the film.

items.body:
Swedish jazz icon Christer Bothén returns to Black Truffle backed by Ghosted's Oren Ambarchi, Johan Berthling and Andreas Werliin, playing bass clarinet and donso n’goni over the trio's signature kraut-jazz grooves. Hypnotic, trance-inducing biz FFO Natural Information Society, Don Cherry's 'Organic Music Society', Jon Hassell, The Necks.

If you're up on your Swedish jazz, there's no way you won't have stumbled across multi-instrumentalist Bothén. He's still best known for palling around with Don Cherry when the jazz great moved to Scandinavia, even teaching him how to play the donso n'goni, a sacred "hunter's harp" from the Wassoulou region in West Africa that Bothén had picked up when he was in Mali. And he's continued to perform with various local artists and outfits, conspicuously appearing on Ghosted's 2022 debut album just mere moments before Ambarchi's Black Truffle imprint re-issued his lost Afro-fusion classic album 'Trancedance'. Last year, Bothén finally issued his first solo n'goni album and now he's back on Black Truffle with this fleshed-out collaboration with the Ghosted crew, leading Ambarchi's Leslie-cab guitar drones, Berthling's bass and Werliin's drums.

Berthling and Werliin take the lead at first on the title track, hammering out a rotating groove before Bothén lets rip on bass clarinet. And playing a side role, Ambarchi might have the most important presence, using his signature phased, organ-like tones to provide anchoring drones for Bothén's spirited improvisations. He's even more pivotal on 'Antigorite', playing cascading staccato notes over those Leslie moans and creating an rhythmelodic foil for the other three players' more traditional interplay. But it's when Bothén plays the n'ghoni that the album really hits its stride; on 'Lizardite', those buzzing tones offset Ambarchi's crystalline twangs, filling in for Werliin's imposing basslines. It's the moment where everything else just drops into place, creating a structural crescendo before the album careers into darkness on the brilliantly moody closer 'Chrysotile'.

items.body:
Our Darkness descends upon Dark Entries with a reissue of Anne Clark’s epochal proto-house masterpiece from 1984.

"As a young poet, Clark found herself drawn to London’s emerging punk scene. She became acquainted with Psychic TV affiliate David Harrow, with whom she would collaborate on 1983’s Changing Places and 1984’s Joined Up Writing. “Our Darkness,” off the latter album, was released as a single on Ink Records that same year, and became an underground club hit. It’s a singular piece of music: Clark’s lyrics, delivered with equal parts muscular confidence and unease, speak of urban alienation and heartbreak, while Harrow’s production pummels the listener with hydraulic beats and gloom-laced arpeggios. The song’s spirit would prove influential on both the early Chicago house and Detroit techno scenes, where mechanistic funk and existential despair could catalyse dancefloor mayhem.

This reissue offers three versions of “Our Darkness”: the original 12” remix, the Razormaid mix, and a previously unreleased dub version uncovered by David Harrow. Also included is the extended mix of “Sleeper in Metropolis,” another dancefloor hit of Clark’s, as well as the elegiac “Poem for a Nuclear Romance.”

“Our Darkness” channels timeless longing and contemporary dismay, a classic overdue for a little light shed upon it."

items.body:
One of electronic music's most influential recordings, back in circulation.

Most readers of these pages will know the story, but to indulge you with a recap, Gottsching was part of electronic krautrock heroes Ash Ra Tempel and in 1981, off the back of a Klaus Schulze tour, sat down one evening and dropped a continuous piece of music which would uncannily imagine the arc of dance music for a quarter of a century.

Early adopters in the Chicago and Detroit warehouses and mediterranean pleasure palaces must have thrilled to the balanced and continuous surging flow of the hour long piece - even over two sides the mix is perfect for building a club atmosphere and suggesting avenues for mixing, whilst using merely two chords throughout. the minimalism offsets the percussive splendour perfectly - several years later the tune was rediscovered and co-opted into the huge italo house smash Sueno Latino, which cemented its foundation in the burgeoning balearic scene of the time and proceeded through several spells of rapturous revival throughout the nineties, not least when figures like Carl Craig and Basic Channel issued their own radically different reshapes and remakes of the piece.

Very satisfying then to have this Gottsching sanctioned edition, where the game might truly be said to have begun in earnest. As they say on the august walls of the Hardwax emporium - buy or die.

items.body:
Deep club modernist Sa Pa mints his own new label, Dub Techno For Life, with four top drawer cuts of textured, strident pressure tipped FFO classic Chain Reaction x Short Span.

Since 2015 Sa Pa has carved a heads-down path between techno, proper, and its conceptual adjuncts in ambient and sound designer atmospheres, most recently on Short Span and Astral Industries. Now taking matters into his own hands, the ‘Girls on Tour EP’ squares up his most robust club material alongside more experimental urges for a definitive self-portrait displaying a fine spectrum of strengths. 

The four tunes clearly speak to his diversity within a theme, checking for a firm touchstone in Andreas Tilliander aka Mokira with the 10 mins of rolling, claggy heft to ‘Mokira Ultra Dub’, unshelving his 2016 rework for deep ’26 ‘floors, alongside the puckered elegance of ‘Waiting For You’, harking to roots in Teutonic house minimalism, whereas the B-side attends to grubbier urges in the bittersweet, sludgy budge of ‘Modular System’, and lusher, abstract feels on the Actress or Rezzett-esque whorl of ‘World Saving Banger’.

items.body:
Munich’s modern art gallery Museum Brandhorst field wide ranging responses to an exhibit of works and concerts focussed on the works of John Cage, Merce Cunningham, Jasper Johns, Robert Rauschenberg and Cy Twombly, ranging from the sound poetry of Sofia Biazzi; to the sublime levitations of Maria Margolina; avant ambient pop of water lily; the pulsating technoid attack of focus baby; andCaroline Kretschmer’s subaquatic intrigue.

“Museum Brandhorst has invited Sound and Experiment to create a series of performances, audio works, and concerts in relation to the exhibition Fünf Freunde: John Cage, Merce Cunningham, Jasper Johns, Robert Rauschenberg, Cy Twombly. The event took place on June 27, 2025, as part of the Junge Nacht and the opening night of the annual Kunstareal Fest in Munich. The program featured newly produced pieces by Sound and Experiment participants Sofian Biazzi, Ilinca Fechete, focus baby, Daniel Gianfranceschi, Bruno Haas, Caroline Kretschmer, Bradley Leonard, Camilla Metelka, Maria Margolina, rosi and water lily. 

In a preparatory, biweekly seminar, discussions addressed conditions such as spectrotemporal displays, sharing time and frequency domains with different sound pieces simultaneously, and eventual performance constellations. An additional point of departure was a close reading of the indirect role of American artist David Tudor in some of the positions exhibited in Fünf Freunde, the function of the organization E.A.T. (Experiments in Art and Technology), and auditory scene analysis and synthesis in general.

The pieces featured on this CD are related to the presented performances, yet newly produced and with the audio CD format in mind.”

items.body:
An iconic album originally brought to life via Sweden's peerless iDEAL Recordings, Kali Malone’s 'The Sacrificial Code’ is a major work featuring almost two hours of concentrated, creeping organ pieces aligned to non traditional intonation/tuning systems. It's a stunning realisation of ideas borne out of academic and conceptual rigour, with a perception-altering quality that encourages exploration without a preordained endpoint.

The Sacrificial Code’ takes a more surgical approach to the methods first explored on last year’s ‘Organ Dirges 2016 - 2017’. Over the course of three parts performed on three different organs, Malone’s minimalist process captures a jarring precision of closeness, both on the level of the materiality of the sounds and on the level of composition.The recordings here involved careful close miking of the pipe organ in such a way as to eliminate environmental identifiers as far as possible - essentially removing the large hall reverb so inextricably linked to the instrument. The pieces were then further compositionally stripped of gestural adornments and spontaneous expressive impulse -  an approach that flows against the grain of the prevailing musical hegemony, where sound is so often manipulated, and composition often steeped in self indulgence. It echoes Steve Reich’s sentiment “..by voluntarily giving up the freedom to do whatever momentarily comes to mind, we are, as a result, free of all that momentarily comes to mind.”

With its slow, purified and seemingly austere qualities ‘The Sacrificial Code’ guides us through an almost trance-inducing process where we become vulnerable receptors for every slight movement, where every miniature shift in sound becomes magnified through stillness. As such, it’s a uniquely satisfying exercise in transcendence through self restraint and by this point inarguably a modern classic.

items.body:
The eminently watchable Accidental Meetings introduce extended family member, Lovely Dave, with a real guess-again mixtape (the first in a series) refracting myriad strains of blissed synths, outernational jazz, new wave pop, post punk scuzz, screwed club and dub

Six years into Accidental Meetings’ serendipitous plot, we know to expect anything and everything from the Bristol label, so long as it's got a unique soul and does not bore. Lovely Dave ideally plays true to that brief on his 99 minute mixtape, effortlessly glyding from outernational synth folk to a killer Curtis Mayfield cover via everything from thumb piano meditations, jazz-funked sidewinders, and a proto-new beat bomb on the A-side, before swerving from gothic new wave to smudged minimal wave audities, a pitch-slapped batacuda house ace, and meter-messing skronk on the backside.

Brilliantly strange but true!

items.body:
Coltrane’s invigorating ’66 spiritual free jazz salvo - the follow-up to ‘A Love Supreme’ (1965) - is unleashed from the Verve Vault, spotlighting his classic line-up tearing out on templates set by Ornette Coleman years prior, along with more reserved moments of beauty. An evergreen..

"Following the genre-redefining revelations of A Love Supreme in 1965, John Coltrane began a dramatic shift toward spiritual free jazz, abandoning familiar forms in favour of a more abstract sonic palette and bold questions he'd spend the rest of his life and career pursuing. Meditations, released by Impulse! in 1966, continues that emotional throughline while retaining, for the last time in full, the classic quartet that propelled Trane to greatness: pianist McCoy Tyner, bassist Jimmy Garrison and drummer Elvin Jones. (They're further augmented by Pharoah Sanders on tenor sax and additional drummer Rashied Ali.) Meditations pushes Coltrane’s spiritual jazz into heightened realms of energy and abstraction — a powerful document of transformation, intensity, and devotion in Coltrane’s recorded legacy."

This double-LP reissue is the first time that Cuisine will appear on vinyl, with a previously unreleased early version of “Seven of Oceans.” "As originary Aussie industrial legends – although founder Tom Ellard would balk at being branded as such – Severed Heads shaped the continental subcultural sound with their kitchen electronics, chaotic tape loops, and infectious nursery-rhyme-esque mel
items.body:
Severed Heads release an expanded reissue of their 1991 opus Cuisine (With Piscatorial) via Dark Entries. This double-LP reissue is the first time that Cuisine will appear on vinyl, with a previously unreleased early version of “Seven of Oceans.”

"As originary Aussie industrial legends – although founder Tom Ellard would balk at being branded as such – Severed Heads shaped the continental subcultural sound with their kitchen electronics, chaotic tape loops, and infectious nursery-rhyme-esque melodies. Cuisine (With Piscatorial) was the long-running project’s ninth album, and is a commentary on the state of music. Ellard explains: “The whole food joke is really about what music's about and how disposable it is; people have records like they have cups of coffee.” The album also presents a turn away from the dancefloor formalism of the era, which Ellard dismissed as already sufficiently explored. Cuisine brings us punchy pop kernels of the prime Heads variety, all clocking in around three minutes. Cuts like “Pilot in Hell” and “Ugly Twenties” rank among the band’s best through their deadly skewering of synth pop tropes. But the album also offers us a Piscatorial section, where Ellard felt free to “go fishing for ideas.” Here we get a taste of the project’s demented cut-up sensibilities, like on the “Quest for Oom Pa Pa” suite, where vintage jazz records are collaged into an angular nightmare."

items.body:
Marco Cassanelli's latest four-track EP in deep, atmospheric dub techno.

"Rich in warmth, texture and groove, the release finds the Italian producer at his most refined, effortlessly balancing hypnotic rhythms with expansive chord work and immersive sound design that resonates equally on the dancefloor and in more introspective home listening settings.

For more than two decades, Marco Cassanelli has been quietly refining a sound rooted in the deepest traditions of dub techno. Emerging from Rome’s underground electronic scene, he has built a body of work defined by patience, restraint, and a profound understanding of space and atmosphere.

Each track unfolds with patience and purpose, drawing listeners into a world of drifting echoes, subtle movement and finely crafted detail. Rooted firmly in the traditions of dub techno while retaining a distinctive character of its own, the EP is both deeply engaging and beautifully understated—equally suited to late-night club systems and home listening.

The final track introduces an unexpected vocal performance, adding a fresh dimension to the release and bringing the journey to a memorable close.Elegant, timeless and richly textured, this EP is a testament to Cassanelli’s enduring craftsmanship and his ability to create dub techno of the highest calibre."

items.body:
First time reissue of Wolfgang Voigt's foundational first GAS album since its release in 1996 - it remains the archetype for so much contemporary ambient music and back-room techno, melting camouflaged German cultural references into a timeless, anthemic pulse. This new reissue is the original extended vinyl version, with definitive longer versions of the six classic tracks. Available in deluxe 3LP and single CD editions.

By the mid-'90s, techno had become the language of German youth culture, tied up in the country's long history of electronic musical innovation - from Kluster to Kraftwerk - and the revolutionary cry of reunification when the Berlin Wall fell in 1989. Based in Köln, Voigt had already put his stamp on dance music by the time he embarked on the mysterious GAS project, working alongside his brother Reinhard to help devise the sound that would evolve into minimal techno, but GAS felt different - more illusory, hypnotic. 

The name, aside from accurately describing the vaporous ambience that whispers through each track, stands for Germany, Austria, Switzerland, and it was Voigt's concept to not only express the feeling of dropping acid in the Königsforst, a verdant woodland only a short drive from Köln, but to distill centuries of German music into a contemporary haze that reflected a hopeful new era. And after testing the waters with '95's Profan-released EP 'Modern', Voigt set a new benchmark with 'GAS', laying out his narrative over six long movements, the shortest of which clocks in at just under 12 minutes.

Voigt wasn't interested in making songs, exactly, but emphasizing texture, burying samples of traditional German music - from baroque to schlager - in murky drones punctuated by squashed 4/4 rhythms. Not dance music exactly, it's headphone gear that's referencing the dance canon in its shift from the US, through Jamaica and the UK to Germany. Much like the Artificial Intelligence era in the UK, it imprints the familiar cycles (pulsing kick drums, undulating soundsystem-ready basslines) with its own regional character. It's no mistake that Voigt begins with an entirely beatless composition that paints the landscape without revealing the complete palette. The album's airiest track, 'GAS 1' is a stylistic milestone - something we can hear tracking thru electronic music from then until now; just listen to Jan Jelinek, Vladislav Delay, PAN's 'Mono No Aware' comp, or anything on the West Mineral imprint. It's ambient music, but where Eno's vision was trained on an earlier era, Voigt had cut his teeth on acid house, hardcore and Detroit techno, and was able to muddle those influences with his own homegrown obsessions. 

That famous, omnipresent filtered kick makes its first appearance on 'GAS 2', thudding beneath watery glitches and sweeping orchestral pads. Voigt doesn't make his concept too vivid (at least at this stage in its evolution), but the outline of classical music is there, punctured by mesmerising minimal thuds that as yet hadn't become a meme. It's not music that develops, it exists, freezing a moment in time and letting the mind pick out a scene, concentrating on the organic, shifting harmonies rather than the static beat. If acid house was all about the squelch, this was all about vapour, as sample-rich pads seem to disappear into clouds of static, blooming from the density. There's a more evident schlager-inspired swing on 'GAS 4' that Voigt and his Kompakt crew would explore more in the coming years, but it's contorted into a subterranean rumble, and on 'GAS 5', the producer tentatively glances trance's quivering euphoria, using reverb and delay to turn anthemic stabs into whooshing melodic rushes. 

If you haven't managed to hear GAS before, this is the perfect starting point, and if you've only heard the album in its truncated form (both the CD release and the 'Nah und Fern' version were incomplete), then we've got to say this is the one.

items.body:
In the 15+ years that have elapsed since 'Loop Finding Jazz Records' first shuffled out of his ambrosially dusty speakers, Jan Jelinek's most famous album has acquired an almost mythical status. Originally released via Pole's defunct Scape imprint, it now finds new life via Jelinek's own Faitiche label, for a new generation to marvel at one of the finest examples of loop-based electronic music typical of the early noughties.

Taking what reads like a pretty austere set of ingredients, Jelinek's technique revolves around a trio of elements which consist of second long cuts of 1960's-70's jazz recordings, the loop-finding modulation wheel (do your homework!) and the Moiré effect; albeit rendered in the acoustic as opposed to the image and spectral domains.

If all this sounds a bit academic, be assured that on record it is anything but; as crumbling edifices of mealy rhythms slowly pulse into life and swirl around your head like snow storms clashing with a dust devil. Taking sediments of fathom deep static then skimming the best stuff from the top, Jelinek opens through the dampened echoes of 'Moiré (piano & organ)' wherein a slow-motion thrum of spiraling clicks, rustles and analogue tones conspire to give the impression of recondite perspectives that extend well beyond the constituent elements.

Elsewhere, 'Rocky in the Video Age' instills a gratuitously optimistic blush to the aquatic micro-sound ebb, 'Moiré (Strings)' is a perfect companion to Basinski's disintegrating tape archive, whilst 'Them, Their' represents an aural crease so sleight you can only catch its distinctive gleam from the corner of your eye.

items.body:
Finally, Kompakt issue a true GAS outlier on vinyl for the first time, recorded in 1989 and containing some of Wolfgang Voigt’s earliest and starkest recycling of magisterial Wagner loops, closest to the ends of The Caretaker, Philip Jeck, Kevin Drumm.

One of those releases that has lurked on our shelves since 2008 as a book and CD, ‘November 89’ exists in the margins of Wolfgang Voigt’s GAS canon as its creepiest and most occluded evocation of long walks in the Bavarian forests. While other GAS classics ooze a sort of dappled warmth breaking thru the trees in their widescreen dub techno strolls, you can fully feel the light dying over the horizon and the forest drawing in on this particularly gloomy, hour-long suite. 

As the title suggests, it was mostly, remarkably, made in ’89, back when Voigt was finding his feet between techno, house and indie-pop, and nearly a decade before he co-founded Kompakt with Michael Mayer & Jürgen Paape - by which time he was a full-fledged rave dynamo as Love Inc. and myriad others notable projects. And, in that sense, it can be heard as his ‘Selected Ambient Works 89-95’ - or perhaps more pertinently with SAW II vibes - in his nascent attempt to chase the ambient dragon, which surely endures for its strangely nostalgic, unheimlich qualities.

An educated guess leads us to think the first three were made in ’89, taking in the nightfall scenery of smudged symphonic strings and icy crackle to ‘Der Wald’, plus the muddied bass waltz and spectral pall of ‘Das Moor’, thru the self-evidently titled centrepiece ‘1989-11-01’, bristling with a digitally iridescent dread. ‘Tal 90’ and ‘Nah Und Fern’, which shares its title with the 2008 boxset, were most likely made a little later, and find the wintry doom thawing to the GAS-eous forms we’ve all come to deeply know and adore. 

A true evergreen for deep ambient techno connoisseurs, no less

items.body:
On Kirk Barley’s definitive solo gem, alternative tunings and a tactile feel for pitching rhythms generate their gentlest and most absorbing work, twinkling amid a microcosm of similar, exploratory productions from Mark Fell & Rian Treanor thru to Aleksi Perälä, Beatrice Dillon, Terry Riley & Jon Hassell.

Building on a decade of work spanning cuts for Brownswood thru to jams with Matthew Herbert and Matt Davies, ‘Arc’ finds Yorkshire-bred artist Barley fully indulge formative passions for microtonal just intonation - as seeded in Terry Riley’s ‘Shri Camel’ - and slippery syncopation to the fullest. Half solo, proper, and half peppered with percussion by regular spar, Matt Davies, it follows his nose for open frontiers of alternative tunings and wonky meter with the blend of low key modesty and prism-pushing tekkerz that have long endeared his work to lovers of lower case experimental music. 

Sweetly balanced between timeless, folk-soul-wise and futurist sensibilities, the half hour suite knits hyaline synths and rippling gamelan metallophonics with clarinet and guitar in lissom, sloshing shapes that effortlessly seduce, rather than demand, the listener’s attention. In particular we are drawn to the bits in duo with Davies, floating sublime ideas in the dreamlike, inverted dub architexture of ‘Ion’, settling on mind like a strangely bucolic Incus work on ’Sundry’, and thru the exquisite, tip-toed rhythms of ‘Ecstatic’, to a trippier, bittersweet type of ante-chamber music on ‘Fret (Hear)’.

He’s also deeply charming when left to his own devices. Ambient opener ‘Billow’ calls to mind the tenderness of Cotton Goods works, and ‘Knead’ chases a certain geist of Irdial or Plaid-esque gamelantronica into the sublime title tune, while ‘Prism’ most beautifully ties all his interests in a melting dream sequence which he caps with the harmonic nightlight glow of ‘Column’.

items.body:
'I Bet on Sky' is the third Dinosaur Jr. album since the original trio – J Mascis, Lou Barlow and Murph – reformed in 2005 and it marks the band’s 10th studio album since their debut on Homestead Records in 1985. 

"Back in the ‘80s, if anyone has suggested that these guys would be performing and recording at such a high level 27 years later, they would have been laughed out of the tree fort.

The trio has taken everything they’ve learned from the various projects they tackled over the years, and poured it directly into their current mix. J’s guitar approaches some of its most unhinged playing here, but there’s a sense of instrumental control that matches the sweet murk of his vocals (not that he always remembers to exercise control on stage, but that’s another milieu). This is head-bobbing riff-romance at the apex. Lou’s basswork shows a lot more melodicism now as well, although his two songs on I Bet on Sky retain the jagged rhythmic edge that has so often marked his work. And Murph…well, he still pounds the drums as hard and as strong as a pro wrestler, with deceptively simple structures that manage to interweave themselves perfectly with his bandmates’ melodic explosions.

After submerging myself in I Bet on Sky, it’s clear that the album is a true and worthy addition to the Dinosaur Jr. discography. It hews close enough to rock formalism to please the squares. Yet it is brilliantly imprinted with the trio’s magical equation, which is a gift to the rest of us. For a combo that began as anomalous fusion of hardcore punk and pop influences, Dinosaur Jr. have proven themselves to be unlikely masters of the long game."

items.body:
Ambient composer Natalia Beylis leads an ensemble of Nyahh’s finest in her landscape-shaped evocation of a field in Leitrim, Éire, quietly meditating on the natural logic of birds and trees.

‘Around Here The Birds Plant The Trees’ is Beylis’ slow-burn, long-form arrangement for quintet - Eimear Reidy (cello), Tola Custy (fiddle), Ailbhe Nic Oireachtaigh & Ultan O’Brien (violin), and Willie Stewart (percussion) - seeded in her reading of a blackbird’s dawn chorus, and subsequent conversation with a local farmer on how “birds are the architects of the living landscape”. It follows some 40 solo albums over the past 20 years (not to mention jams with Woven Skull and Tomuttontu) with a considered approach to what lies just beyond her home; typically drawing on her attentive reading of the rural soundsphere to transmute the poetry of birdsong and the natural world into expressive musical metaphor.

The low bowed cello tone of regular spar Eimear Reidy underlines and opens out a breezy space where where the fiddle and violinists criss-cross air in reserved melodic flight and plucky figures that alternate like the play of light on Ireland’s remote North West. The piece unfolds to boggy pockets of percussion and passages of barely-there, hushed gloam, as though the wind itself was generating the players’ gestures, which rise to cloud castle hover around the midway, only to depart for Nyahh label boss Willie Stewart’s rolling drum thunder and scrape of Ailbhe Nic Oireachtaigh's fiddle rooted in the rolling landscape. Ultimately the folk soul of the turf rises in its final section, resembling a rousing, swaying folk song voiced by the strings in ideally creaky discord.

items.body:
Simply lovely come-down aids by OTTO Benson, leading on from his acclaimed 2020 turn on Vegyn’s PLZ Make It Ruins with a reminder of his slept-on gem from late ’22, reissued on the NYC label behind last year’s ‘Peanut’ tape. FFO Tenniscoats, early AFX, ’00s electronica

True to the brief, Otto follows his nose for charming melodic ribbons tied in burbling rhythms across ‘Songs Before Bed’. In clearly separated halves, the first lot revolves pared-back, gently psyched guitar blessed with a sun-dazed wooze that flows from his phasing, tremolo effected licks on ‘River Dream’ thru hints of Bibio on ‘Another Long day’, and cute vignette ‘Orange Moon’. The other half is more akin his work on Vegyn’s label, sharing a timeless melodic appeal with its boss as much as sweeter ends o ‘90s AFX in the procession from endearingly naïf hook and lilting drum machine to ‘Jumping Seeds’, thru  delectable, beat-less ambient shimmer in ‘Histamine’ and the supine bewt ‘Tuning In and Out’, to the gauzy strokes of ‘Good Night Mantra’.

items.body:
Josephine Foster and The Victor Herrero Band release "Anda Jaleo / Pearlas" via Fire Records.

"Anda Jaleo was originally released in 2010. Federico Garcia Lorca's popular folk song collection "Las Canciones Populares Espanolas" was banned under Franco's dictatorship and today the music survives but marginally within the Spanish sub-conscious. Taking their cue from Lorca and La Argentinita's infectious 1931 recording of the songs, Josephine Foster and her partner Spanish musician Victor Herrero arranged the poetically rich collection for their acoustic band, formed while living in the Grenadine Sierra. Anda Jaleo is the band's live recording of "Las Canciones"; a visceral celebration of the persistence of popular anonymous song. This new edition includes an additional track not featured on the original release, an interpretation of ‘Sones de Asturias’. La colección de "Canciones Populares Españolas" recopiladas y armonizadas por Federico García Lorca fue censurada en tiempos de Franco, y hoy en día la música sobrevive aunque de una manera vaga en el subconsciente del pueblo español. Inspirados por la contagiosa grabación de las canciones de Lorca y La Argentinita de 1931, Josephine Foster y su compañero el músico español Víctor Herrero han arreglado esta poética y rica colección para su banda acústica , formada mientras vivían en la sierra de Granada. Anda Jaleo es la grabación en directo de su versión de "Las Canciones"; una celebración visceral de la canción popular anónima y su persistencia. Following from Anda Jaleo, Josephine Foster and the Victor Herrero Band created a superb follow-up entitled Perlas (Pearls). It is a jewel of a collection, with songs and poems selected by Josephine herself, gathered from dusty old scores and brought vividly to the present with warm performances full of flesh-and-blood emotion. Made with a variety of stringed instruments and simple percussion, the songs were recorded live in the studio on to analogue tape by Paco Loco in Puerto de Santa Maria, Spain. Foster breathes new life into timeless traditional melodies, drawing from the Spanish-folk traditions of Castile, the Basque, Santander and the Costa Brava."

items.body:
Beirut-based sound artist and veteran improviser Jad Atoui captures his country's current instability on his latest full-length, performing live in situ with his modular rig.

Ostensibly a noise record, it's inspired by Atoui's early club experiences, where he twigged the physicality of sound for the first time. Here, he uses the same properties to provoke very different responses, layering distorted waves of sound on 'Pressure Dream' that might as well be collapsing buildings. And by recording the material live, there's a distinct human touch that's often missing from this kind of material. Atoui is able to work instinctively, reacting to the sound in the room on the outstanding 'Reaching Heart' as glassy drones bend to corroded rhythmic interjections. 

There's even a glimmer of hope; the gorgeous 'Blue Moon Red Cloud' is a break from stuttering beats and searing noise that hits like an oasis in the desert, lifted by Atoui's freeform melodies and delirious FM chimes.

items.body: Label: Biophilia Records, 2026 Personnel - Linda May Han Oh: double bass; Melissa Aldana: tenor saxophone. Bassist Linda May Han Oh and saxophonist Melissa Aldana are two respected bandleaders and composers with different styles and approaches but common journeys in life. Oh was born in Malaysia to parents of Chinese heritage, was raised in Australia, and moved to New York for a brilliant career, having played with Pat Metheny, Vijay Iyer, Joe Lovano, and Dave Douglas, among many others. Aldana is a native of Santiago, Chile, and has lived in New York since 2009, after graduating from Berklee College of Music. For this session, the duo agreed to play standards, showcasing reverence for jazz tradition and influences while also allowing new possibilities to emerge from the arrangements. Yet Beneath Lifted Skies also includes three duo improvisations and three solo bass tracks. Charlie Parker’s “ Anthropology ” comes out of the gate with a vibrantly swinging mood, swift unisons, and exciting exchanges infused with a richness of ideas. Yet it doesn’t beat the fantastic rendition of Bud Powell’s “ Hallucinations ”, where the duo is at its best. Impressive synchronization, great melody, and a grooving, energizing vibe are part of a breathtaking interplay that demonstrates Oh’s immaculate technique and Aldana’s fluid language. Ballads where melody reigns, such as Charles Mingus’ “ Duke Ellington’s Sound of Love ” and Sammy Fain’s “ I’ll Be Seeing You ”, make a great pair. Aldana’s quick-witted, arpeggiated sequences à la Charles Lloyd put a smokiness in the air. In turn, pieces by jazz giants Wayne Shorter (“ Dance Cadaverous ”) and John Coltrane (“ 26-2 ”) didn’t impress me as much. One that really gets under the skin is Gigi Gryce’s “ Social Call ”, a graceful, easy-rolling tune expressed with joyful hookiness. Of the three improvised pieces, “ Infinite ” is the one that caught my ear instantly, relying on droning pedals and searching melodies to take us to a progressive yet atmospheric place. “ Resolve ”, which ends with a pedaling bass figure, also makes for a compelling abstract sonic painting. Oh absolutely excels on her solo reframing of Herbie Hancock’s “ The Sorcerer ”, where edginess and roundness go together, creating an almost subliminal pulse. The bassist also tackles Billie Holiday’s “ God Bless the Child ”, delivered as a protest against child abuse, and introduces a new composition, “ Winter ”, where she employs expert pulses and slides to add novelty. Demonstrating a quick-witted rapport, Oh and Aldana are two kindred spirits in conversation. They’ve already found their own voices in jazz, but together, they manage to offer a very enjoyable album with varied rhythm, groove, and breath. While old standards can sometimes feel stale, creative reinvention transforms them into a thrilling experience. Beneath Lifted Skies is an excellent case in point. Favorite Tracks: 02 - Hallucinations ► 03 - Improvisation: Infinite ► 06 - The Sorcerer ► 10 - Social Call

items.body:
P-pop took over Japan as BINI and SB19 brought Filipino music to Summer Sonic on 14 and 16 August, performing across the festival’s Osaka and Tokyo editions.

For BINI, the weekend marked the eight-member girl group’s Summer Sonic debut. They first took the Mountain Stage at Expo ’70 Commemorative Park in Osaka on 14 August, before heading to Tokyo’s Mountain Stage at ZOZO Marine Stadium and Makuhari Messe on 16 August.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by BINI_ph (@bini_ph)

Across their 40-minute sets, BINI ran through fan favourites including 'Cherry on Top', 'Zero Pressure', 'Out of My Head', 'Blush', and 'Step Back'. They also gave the Japanese crowd something made especially for the occasion, performing a Japanese version of 'Born to Win' and incorporating Japanese lines into 'Salamin, Salamin', before closing with 'Pantropiko'. Osaka also heard 'Sugar Rush', while the Tokyo audience got 'Unang Kilig'.

The performances travelled beyond the festival grounds, too. BINI reached No. 1 and No. 3 on X’s global trends during their Osaka and Tokyo appearances, respectively, while also topping Philippine trends on both days.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by BINI_ph (@bini_ph)

Over at Summer Sonic Osaka, SB19 brought their high-energy live show to Expo ’70 Commemorative Park on 14 August. Pablo, Josh, Stell, Felip, and Justin opened with 'DAM', worked 'Quit' and 'Memories' into their set, and closed with 'Crimzone'.

“We stepped onto the stage ready to give it our all, and you gave us even more energy in return,” the group shared after the performance. “Osaka, thank you for an unforgettable Day 1.”

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by SB19 Official (@officialsb19)

SB19 returned for Summer Sonic Tokyo on 16 August with a special surprise: Japanese singer and actor Kento Nakajima joined them for 'GENTO', delivering his own Japanese verse and taking on the song’s choreography alongside the group. The collaboration followed a previous meet-up between the artists, which SB19 teased ahead of the festival by saying that “something might be in the works.”

The Tokyo set also saw SB19 add 'I Want You' and 'Moonlight' to their festival repertoire. Their Summer Sonic run came a month after another international milestone, when they became the first Filipino group to perform at Lollapalooza.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by SB19 Official (@officialsb19)

Together, BINI and SB19’s Summer Sonic appearances put two of P-pop’s biggest names in front of audiences in Japan on the same festival weekend — each bringing their own sound, performance style, and fandom energy to the global stage.

items.body:
After more than seven decades, Columbia House is calling it a day.

The long-running mail-order media club will stop accepting new orders after 15 September, according to a notice on its website. Customers will still be able to purchase books using existing credits or credit cards.

The closure brings an end to a 71-year run for a company that once changed how millions of people discovered and bought music from home.

Founded in 1955 as the Columbia Record Club by CBS/Columbia Records, the service offered records through the mail, allowing listeners to build their collections without heading to a record store. By 1963, it reportedly accounted for 10% of the music retail market.

Columbia House later expanded its catalogue by licensing releases from other labels and evolved alongside the formats music fans were buying, from vinyl records to cassettes and CDs.

For a generation of listeners, the company became synonymous with offers promising a stack of albums for next to nothing — including its memorable deal of as many as 12 CDs for a penny. The catch was that members would subsequently purchase releases at full price, with the service also using a controversial practice known as “negative option billing”, under which customers could be charged for selections unless they opted out.

At its height in 1996, Columbia House counted 16 million members. That same year, it launched its website as music retail began its shift online.

The decades that followed were considerably rockier. Sony sold half of Columbia House to Time Warner in 1991, while subsequent years saw the company change hands multiple times as online retailers, big-box stores and digital music reshaped the way audiences bought and consumed music.

Competitor BMG acquired Columbia House in 2005 and consolidated its operations. Following another acquisition in 2008, the business was renamed Direct Brands, which eventually ended its music mail-order operations while continuing to sell DVDs and Blu-rays under the Columbia House name.

Its Canadian operation ceased business in 2010, while the US company filed for bankruptcy in 2015. Plans were later floated to revive Columbia House as a vinyl subscription service amid the format's resurgence, but the comeback did not materialise.

Sony Music continues to own the Columbia House trademark, while Edge Line Ventures LLC is its current licensee.

For music fans who remember leafing through catalogues and choosing which albums would arrive at their doorstep next, Columbia House's closure marks the end of a distinctly pre-streaming way of discovering and collecting music.

The three-night waterfront celebration will bring together live performances, food pop-ups, community booths, and fundraising activities, with Singaporean musicians taking the stage throughout the weekend.

RRILEY will headline the Festival's opening night on 28 August. The Singaporean artist, who first made her debut as a founding member of local pop quartet The Sam Willows, will perform alongside Thye Hua Kwan Moral Charities' Brave Hearts Ensemble, an inclusive performing arts group formed by residents of THK Home for the Disabled at Eunos.

Local bands 53A, The Vibes, and SuperSonic will also soundtrack the weekend with live renditions of cover favourites.

Beyond the music, festival-goers can head to the Good Bites Market, where five gourmet pop-up experiences will raise funds for non-profit organisation AWWA and its Enabled Living @ Bedok programme, which aims to empower individuals with disabilities to live independently.

Black Tap Craft Burgers & Beer, Bread Street Kitchen, and RISE will serve up specially priced dishes and drinks, while Roberta's Pizza and homegrown Café Nesuto will join the Festival for the first time.

Black Tap Craft Burgers & Beer;The All-American Burger

Visitors can also participate in Impact Match, an interactive game where players create digital school packs containing essential supplies. Each successfully completed pack will be matched by Marina Bay Sands with a school pack for students at NorthLight School.

Meanwhile, the Giving Marketplace will bring together local non-profits, social enterprises, and small businesses, including APSN, ART:DIS, Cat Welfare Society, MINDS, Carer, Social Gifting, Teddy Thotz, and more.

The annual Community Chest Heartstrings Walk and Race to the Sky Vertical Marathon will also return on 29 August. Co-organised by Marina Bay Sands and Community Chest, the event includes a walk around Marina Bay and a 57-storey vertical climb to the SkyPark Observation Deck, supporting more than 300 social service programmes across Singapore.

Giving Marketplace

Dine for Good returns throughout August

The Festival's fundraising efforts will extend beyond Event Plaza with Dine for Good, which runs from 1 to 30 August.

12 signature and celebrity chef restaurants at Marina Bay Sands will each dedicate proceeds from a selected dish to AWWA's Enabled Living @ Bedok programme.

Among the dishes on offer are LAVO's Reginette Seafood Alfredo at S$45++, Yardbird's Chicken & Waffles at S$48++, Maison Boulud's Coq Au Vin at S$42++, and Origin + Bloom's Chicken Rendang Sandwich at S$12 nett.

LAVO Coastal Italian Restaurant and Rooftop Bar; Reginette Seafood Alfredo

Miracle Coffee will also collaborate with Marina Bay Sands' pastry team on a KIKU-inspired matcha and yuzu cake, available exclusively from 10 to 30 August.

Speaking about the initiative, Huixia See Toh, Director of Family Services at AWWA, said: “We look forward to this continued support for AWWA’s latest initiative, Enabled Living @ Bedok, which will empower persons with disabilities to live independently and participate actively in the community with confidence and dignity.”

Since launching in 2013, Sands for Singapore Charity Festival has helped raise more than S$45 million for social causes in Singapore, supporting low-income families, youths, seniors, and persons with disabilities.

“By connecting these experiences with opportunities to give back, we hope to inspire even more people to support causes that matter to Singapore while strengthening the social bonds that help communities thrive,” said Paul Town, Chief Operating Officer at Marina Bay Sands.

items.body:
Singapore-based live entertainment platform Triangle Group has raised US$15 million in funding as it looks to make touring across Asia-Pacific easier for artists and their teams.

The investment comprises a US$10 million equity seed round led by DSG Consumer Partners and US$5 million in venture debt from Genesis Alternative Ventures.

Headquartered in Singapore, Triangle Group currently operates across 18 cities in nine countries, with teams in Singapore, Australia, Malaysia, and Indonesia. Its goal is to tackle one of the longstanding challenges of touring Asia-Pacific: connecting individual markets into viable regional touring routes.

For artists with established fanbases in Asia, mounting a multi-city tour can involve navigating different promoters, visa requirements, tax systems, languages, and audience spending power from market to market.

Zaran Vacha

“Every city in Asia is completely different,” shared Triangle Group co-founder Zaran Vachha. “When we send a proposal to a London agent, they're dealing with one counterparty who actually knows Jakarta, Manila, and Melbourne.”

Vachha has spent two decades developing touring circuits across Asia, working with acts ranging from Pharrell Williams to underground electronic artists. He is joined by co-founder Greg Hargrave, an Australian entrepreneur with experience in fintech and ASX-listed companies, and Chief Financial Officer Matthew Qi-Tao.

The company has also brought former Live Nation Asia Pacific President Roger Field onboard as Executive Director and Operating Partner. Field previously served as CEO of Live Nation Australia & New Zealand and spent a year as an advisor and investor in Triangle before joining the company full-time.

“Running Live Nation across this region taught me one thing: Asia-Pacific doesn't need a global template; it needs an operator who understands every market individually,” said Field.

Roger Field

“That's the business we're building at Triangle—applying global standards with a regional focus. There's a larger piece of the pie we can claim by making it genuinely easier to tour the region.”

Triangle operates a portfolio of live entertainment brands, including Collective Minds, Curious, and Touch Bass.

Collective Minds has worked on tours and events featuring artists including Fred again.., Jamie xx, Charlotte de Witte, Black Coffee, Kamasi Washington, Eric Prydz, and Wolf Alice, alongside festival properties such as A State of Trance (ASOT) and S2O.

Curious focuses on live speaking tours and recently brought The Diary of a CEO author Steven Bartlett to Asia, while Touch Bass operates a multi-city drum & bass touring festival in Australia.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Pitch Control (@pitchcontrolau)

Triangle's wider touring roster has also included HONNE, Hanumankind, Gilles Peterson, James Hype, and Boris Brejcha, among others.

Upcoming events under the group's brands include Singapore shows from The Martinez Brothers, ARTBAT, Intercell, and Dom Dolla, alongside Intercell in Hong Kong and Otherworld Festival in Manila. Its Australian operations also have Tomorrowland CORE in Melbourne and Rampage dates across Australia and New Zealand on the calendar.

According to Triangle Group, Asia-Pacific's live entertainment market is projected to reach US$75 billion by 2033, while the region is expected to account for almost two-thirds of the world's middle class by 2035.

With its latest funding, the company is positioning itself around that growing appetite for live experiences — building the regional infrastructure to make more Asia-Pacific tour stops commercially and operationally possible for artists.

items.body:
Taipei is gearing up for four days of music, industry exchange, and cross-border discovery as TAIPEI MUSIC EXPO (TMEX) returns to Taipei Music Center from 27 to 30 August.

Held under the theme "Tune in to Taiwan. Sync with Asia.", this year's edition will bring together more than 100 music industry professionals from 15 markets alongside over 60 exhibiting brands from across the region. TMEX will also run alongside its music festival, JAM JAM ASIA, which takes over the weekend of 29 and 30 August with more than 80 acts from 14 markets performing across seven stages.

The expo continues its focus on connecting Taiwan's music scene with the wider Asia-Pacific and global music industries through five pillars: brand exhibitions, business matching, forums, emerging talent showcases, and fan engagement. The first two days will be reserved for industry delegates before the programme opens to the public over the weekend.

TMEX's wider platform is designed to bring artists, audiences, and markets together through its exhibition, forum, festival, and networking programmes, with technology and sustainability identified as key areas of focus.

The team behind KPop Demon Hunters comes to Taipei

Among the highlights of this year's TMEX Forum is a session featuring members of the team behind Netflix's KPop Demon Hunters.

Director Maggie Kang, producer Michelle Wong, and THEBLACKLABEL songwriter Danny Chung, who is also the voice of Baby Saja, will discuss what the film could mean for Asia-Pacific artists looking to enter global markets.

Grammy-winning mastering engineer Howie Weinberg will also make his Taiwan debut with a session exploring the sonic aesthetics behind his work across 9,000 records.

Elsewhere, festival programmers from the US, UK, Korea, Japan, and Taiwan will come together to discuss how festivals develop their identities, audiences, and international partnerships. Other sessions will tackle generative AI in music production with Suno and KKBOX, international artist marketing, and sustainability in live events.

Beyond the forum, TMEX will connect artists and music businesses with international curators and buyers, bringing together festivals, labels, management companies, digital platforms, and music-related brands.

This year's participating organisations include Goldenvoice, Live Nation, Fuji Rock Festival, Summer Sonic, YG PLUS, Zandari Festa, MPMG, Zepp, Beggars Group, and Secretly Group. Music export agencies will also join the exhibition floor, including Thailand's Creative Economy Agency, Vietnam Cultural Industry Development Association, Sounds Australia, and Taiwan's TAICCA.

JAM JAM ASIA brings over 80 acts to seven stages

For fans, the weekend belongs to JAM JAM ASIA.

Taking place across 29 and 30 August, the festival will feature more than 80 acts from 14 markets, spanning everything from Japanese city pop and Indonesian metal to Thai indie and Kazakh electronic music. Performances will unfold across seven stages, including four indoor air-conditioned halls, a 3,000-capacity outdoor stage, free stages spotlighting emerging artists, and late-night DJ takeovers.

Leading the lineup is Japanese city pop pioneer Taeko Onuki, alongside HYUKOH, who will perform with Kuo of Sunset Rollercoaster.

Also joining the bill are Filipino-American neo-soul artist ((( O ))), Indonesian metal trio Voice of Baceprot, Bangkok rapper Réjizz, Korean-Australian rap collective 1300, Seoul indie band HOA, Japanese four-piece ATARASHII GAKKO!, and Japanese hip-hop producer DJ KRUSH.

Taiwan's own scene will also be represented by acts including Elephant Gym and Amazing Show, while JAM JAM ASIA's international partnerships will bring additional cross-border showcase acts to Taipei, including TV Tairiku Ondo via Fuji Rock Festival.

With its mix of industry conversations, international networking, emerging talent, and a sprawling weekend festival, TMEX is positioning Taipei as a meeting point for music scenes from across the Asia-Pacific.

items.body:
CORTIS have wrapped their first-ever North American tour on a high, selling out every stop of 2026 CORTIS TOUR IN NORTH AMERICA, also known as PUT YOUR PHONE DOWN.

The five-piece — MARTIN, JAMES, JUHOON, SEONGHYEON, and KEONHO — closed out the Live Nation-promoted run with two sold-out nights in San Francisco on 15 and 16 August, following shows in Toronto, New York, Atlanta, Irving, and Los Angeles.

Built around the idea of being fully present at a live show, PUT YOUR PHONE DOWN encouraged fans to experience CORTIS beyond their screens. The concept extended to the group's "PYPD" app, which captured fans' movement and energy throughout the concerts while encouraging them to jump and move along with the performance.

The shows also brought CORTIS closer to their fans, with the members stepping offstage to perform within the crowd. Each stop featured its own touches, including the group sporting cowboy hats during their Irving show.

Across the tour, CORTIS performed tracks including 'YOUNGCREATORCREW', 'FaSHioN', 'REDRED', 'ACAI', 'JoyRide', 'Lullaby', and 'Blue Lips'. Their Juicy J collaboration, 'MOTION (feat. Juicy J)', also made the setlist after receiving its live debut at Lollapalooza Chicago.

The tour followed CORTIS' Lollapalooza Chicago debut on 1 August, where they took over the T-Mobile Stage in front of approximately 50,000 festivalgoers. Clips from the rain-soaked performance gained traction online and helped introduce the group to new audiences.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Lollapalooza (@lollapalooza)

CORTIS have since become the fastest K-pop group to reach 15 million Instagram followers. The group have also amassed 16.3 million followers on TikTok and 6.3 million YouTube subscribers, which BIGHIT MUSIC says are the highest figures among K-pop boy groups that debuted within the past five years.

The momentum has carried over to the charts. CORTIS' second EP, GREENGREEN, jumped 75 places on the Billboard 200, moving from No. 114 to No. 39 in its 13th week on the chart.

Following their North American run, CORTIS will celebrate their first anniversary with the 2026 CORTIS TOUR BIRTHDAY PARTY on 22 and 23 August in Seoul.

The group are also set to return to Southeast Asia later this year, taking the stage at the Formula 1 Singapore Grand Prix on 9 October.

items.body:
The Recording Academy has signalled that it may reconsider its newly introduced Asian Pop GRAMMY category, following criticism from artists and BTS' decision not to submit their music for the upcoming awards.

Recording Academy CEO Harvey Mason Jr. addressed concerns surrounding the category in a statement, acknowledging that some artists do not feel adequately represented by the award.

“It’s clear from our numerous conversations with many stakeholders over the past two weeks that, regardless of our intent and desire to be even more inclusive, there are some artists in this space who feel that this category isn’t representing the music they work so hard to create, in the way they wish,” Mason said in a statement to Billboard.

“As a musician myself, I take that to heart.”

According to Variety, Mason and other GRAMMY executives have been holding discussions with artists and industry representatives across K-pop, J-pop, C-pop, Indian music, and other Asian music communities. The Recording Academy is also reportedly convening its full Board and Awards & Nominations Committee to seek further input on the category and the process through which new GRAMMY categories are introduced.

The development comes after BTS announced on 29 July that they would not submit their music for GRAMMY consideration. In identical statements shared by the members, the group expressed their hope that “music can be heard and loved by itself rather than being divided by region or language.”

The statement was widely interpreted as criticism of the GRAMMYs' new Asian Pop category, which was introduced amid the continued global growth of music from Asia.

The category has since sparked debate over whether creating a region-specific award provides greater representation for Asian artists or instead separates them from established genre and General Field categories. Reports noted that genre-specific categories can face similar criticism when artists feel they are being confined to a particular classification rather than being considered alongside the wider field.

While the Recording Academy has yet to announce any official changes, Mason said its management and Board were committed to ensuring the artists the GRAMMYs intended to recognise “feel truly seen and heard by our actions.”

The Academy's response marks the latest development in the conversation surrounding Asian music's place within major global awards institutions — and whether increasingly borderless pop music should continue to be classified according to geography.

items.album: BLACKPINK apologise to BLINKs following criticism over 10th anniversary celebrations
items.excerpt:
BLACKPINK have addressed fans following criticism surrounding the K-pop group’s 10th anniversary celebrations, with JISOO, ROSÉ, LISA, and JENNIE each sharing messages with BLINKs after the milestone.

The quartet marked their 10th anniversary on 8 August, a decade after making their debut. However, what was meant to be a celebratory moment became a source of disappointment for some fans, who raised concerns over the scale, organisation, and communication surrounding the anniversary activities.
items.body:
BLACKPINK have addressed fans following criticism surrounding the K-pop group’s 10th anniversary celebrations, with JISOO, ROSÉ, LISA, and JENNIE each sharing messages with BLINKs after the milestone.

The quartet marked their 10th anniversary on 8 August, a decade after making their debut. However, what was meant to be a celebratory moment became a source of disappointment for some fans, who raised concerns over the scale, organisation, and communication surrounding the anniversary activities.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by BLΛƆKPIИK (@blackpinkofficial)

At the centre of the criticism was an anniversary event held at the National Museum of Korea in Seoul’s Yongsan District. According to reports, the event was announced two days beforehand and was attended by 40 fans selected from paid Weverse membership holders.

All four BLACKPINK members ultimately attended the gathering, which included interactions with fans, flowers, and a three-tiered pink cake. The group also appeared together for a brief livestream.

However, the relatively intimate scale of the event — alongside earlier uncertainty over whether all four members would be present and the limited advance notice — left some BLINKs disappointed. Reports described the livestream as lasting around 10 minutes and the main programme around 30 minutes.

JISOO addresses BLINKs during anniversary celebrations

[TRANS] jisoo: We really wanted to meet a lot of fans, and we know how important our 10th anniversary is. But I think there were some issues with our communication and we’re very sorry about that. We really wanted to spend the day happily with joy and we want to say that we…

— BLACKPINK BLINK UNION 💕 (@BBU_BLACKPINK) August 8, 2026

JISOO was among the first members to address the response from fans.

During the livestream, she acknowledged that communication surrounding the anniversary could have been better and apologised to BLINKs who had been left disappointed.

“I originally wanted to see so many of you, and I knew this was an important day — our 10th anniversary,” she said. “I wanted this to be a happy occasion, but I’m sorry to the BLINKs who feel let down. I hope you know that I love you.”

After footage of JISOO becoming emotional while reading fan letters prompted speculation online, she later asked fans to refrain from negative discussion and “baseless speculation” surrounding the anniversary.

ROSÉ says she wanted the anniversary to be a day everyone could celebrate

ROSÉ subsequently shared a longer message with fans, explaining that she had needed time to gather her thoughts.

The singer said she understood BLINKs’ disappointment and apologised for potentially making fans “feel even more alone” by not speaking sooner.

Reflecting on the decade BLACKPINK and BLINKs have spent together, ROSÉ said she had hoped 8 August could simply be a day when the group and its fans could celebrate.

“I wanted Aug. 8, at least, to be a day when all of us could smile and be happy, but things didn’t turn out the way I had hoped, and I’m deeply sorry,” she said.

She also thanked the fans who attended the anniversary gathering despite the hot weather and expressed her hopes for BLACKPINK and BLINKs to continue making memories together.

LISA apologises over how the milestone unfolded

LISA also addressed fans in a message following the anniversary.

The BLACKPINK member said she felt sad about how the milestone had unfolded and apologised to fans, acknowledging that the anniversary was meant to be a special celebration shared between the group and BLINKs.

Rather than offer a justification for what happened, LISA focused her message on the relationship BLACKPINK have built with their fans over the past decade.

Her statement followed those from JISOO and ROSÉ, making her the third member reported to have publicly addressed the disappointment at the time.

JENNIE: “There’s really no excuse I can give for that”

JENNIE followed with her own message to BLINKs on 17 August after completing previously scheduled festival appearances.

Writing on Weverse, she explained that she had been thinking about the anniversary and was saddened that she had not been able to properly speak to fans about how she felt.

“These past 10 years have given me some of the most special moments of my life, all because of you,” JENNIE wrote.

She went on to directly acknowledge the disappointment surrounding the milestone.

“Our 10th anniversary should have been a moment where we could just celebrate and be happy together, and I’m sorry that instead, some of you were left feeling disappointed,” she said. “There’s really no excuse I can give for that.”

JENNIE thanked BLINKs for supporting BLACKPINK throughout the past decade and said she would continue growing and doing her best to return the love the group has received.

BLACKPINK and BLINKs look beyond the anniversary

The controversy arrived during what was intended to be a major milestone for BLACKPINK and their fandom.

Some online criticism also focused on the members’ demeanour during the anniversary livestream. JISOO received praise from some fans for directly addressing concerns, while JENNIE, ROSÉ, and LISA faced criticism from some netizens over how they appeared during the broadcast.

Those reactions, however, reflected interpretations from online commenters rather than statements of intent from the members themselves. All four have since addressed BLINKs in messages acknowledging the disappointment surrounding the anniversary.

For BLACKPINK, the occasion nevertheless marks 10 years shared with a fandom that has followed the group from their 2016 debut to their position as one of K-pop’s biggest global acts.

As ROSÉ put it in her message to fans: “Although all of us were left with some disappointment, I sincerely want to congratulate us once again. Let’s make many more wonderful memories together.”

items.body: Heptaméron 七日譚 is an unusually assured debut, one that embraces the vocabulary of progressive rock while refusing to remain within its boundaries. Built around a fantasy narrative structured by the symbolic recurrence of the number seven, the album unfolds like a journey across an imagined landscape of dungeons, mansions, abysses and forgotten kingdoms, each track functioning as a distinct location within a larger world. Rather than simply borrowing fantasy imagery, Acid Brain 酸腦 use it to organise the album’s musical architecture, allowing motifs and textures to recur, mutate and reappear as the story progresses. The opening “…noise (Heptaméron)” eases the listener into this universe with an unexpectedly gentle flute melody recalling classic progressive rock before “Seven Steps Beneath Dungeon” subjects the same material to a sludge-metal transformation that gradually expands into post-rock. Elsewhere, “Into Mansion” continually shifts its internal momentum without losing its hypnotic pull, while the experimental “Gnome (Interlude)” interrupts the narrative with percussion and electronic chaos. The paired “Abyss I” and “Abyss II” anchor the album firmly within stoner rock, one seeming to decay before reassembling itself, the other acting as its distorted mirror. The emotional core of the album is undoubtedly the sixteen-minute “Maru”. LILLIE CREATURES’ ethereal vocals introduce an unexpected shoegaze inflection before gradually taking on an almost incantatory quality as the piece passes through repeated dynamic transformations. The closing “Requiem”, featuring saxophonist Li Zenghui, pushes the album towards free improvisation and noise, ending not with an overwhelming surge of collective energy. Throughout, Acid Brain 酸腦 demonstrate an impressive command of pacing. Their willingness to juxtapose drone, sludge, post-rock, stoner metal, free jazz, electronics and even chiptune could easily have resulted in a fragmented listen, yet the album remains coherent because every stylistic shift serves its fictional geography rather than functioning as a display of eclecticism. The striking cover artwork by yShin perfectly complements this vision. Depicting a humanoid skull fractured into porous, coral-like structures through vivid psychedelic colours and digital distortion, it occupies the same psychedelic territory as the music itself. Anatomy dissolves into abstraction, suggesting both bodily transformation and altered consciousness. Much like the album, the image constantly oscillates between organic and synthetic, decay and regeneration, marking it as a visual extension of the record’s hallucinatory world. Recorded largely in bedrooms and rehearsal spaces with a DIY ethos, Heptaméron 七日譚 never sounds constrained by its circumstances. Instead, Acid Brain 酸腦 transform limited resources into a remarkably ambitious statement. It is a debut that feels fully realised, confidently mapping out a sonic universe whose borders extend well beyond the conventions of heavy psychedelic rock. To get a taste of Acid Brain 酸腦, here is one of their live sets from 2024. Acid Brain 酸腦 are: Shawn Lee 李想 – acoustic guitar, electric guitar, flute, tin whistle, bass, synthesizer, samples, piano, strings, vocals (tracks 1–9), Eric Lai 賴慶禧 – electric guitar (tracks 2, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9); synthesizer (track 5), Chiayu Hsu 徐嘉佑 – electric guitar, acoustic guitar, synthesizer, samples, vocals (tracks 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9), Yilin Tsai 蔡易霖 – bass, vocals (tracks 2, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9) and Isaac Jiang 江以撒 – drums, percussion (tracks 1–9). To find out more about their album we got in touch directly with them via IG. Heptaméron 七日譚 feels remarkably ambitious for a debut album. Across its nine tracks, you move through drone, stoner rock, post-punk, chiptune, free jazz, post-rock and metal, yet the record never feels like a simple genre exercise. Instead, it unfolds like a coherent fantasy world with its own internal logic. How did the album take shape conceptually, and were there particular books, films, games, myths or musical influences that helped you build this universe of mansions, dungeons, abysses and strange landscapes? From the moment the first song was completed, we decided that this would be a concept album set against a fantasy backdrop. We enjoy embedding symbols within our work, which is why the entire album revolves around the number “7.” The main riff of the opening track is driven by a 7-beat meter, and excluding the intro and interludes, the album consists of exactly seven songs. We are deeply fascinated by the rich world-building in fantasy works, ranging from The Lord of the Rings to The Witcher 3. Influenced heavily by progressive rock concept albums, we wanted to construct a universe of our own. Each track functions like a different location on a vast map, making the entire album a grand tour through this fictional Middle-earth. Although Acid Brain 酸腦 are often described as a heavy psychedelic rock or metal band, Heptaméron 七日譚 incorporates elements that many listeners would not immediately associate with those traditions: flute, tin whistle, synthesizers, chiptune passages, free improvisation and collaborations with artists such as LILLIE CREATURES and Li Zenghui. How did these collaborations come about, and what did those guests bring to the album that you felt could not have been achieved by the band alone? We were completely captivated by Mr. Li Zenghui’s performance when he toured Taipei with Omnipotent Youth Society in 2023. Around that time, he also staged a personal experimental theater piece in Taipei. We fortunately had the opportunity to open for him, which allowed us to extend our invitation. For the album’s finale, “Requiem”, we expanded several sections upon the original foundation to give Mr. Li room to play, and ultimately arranged a free-tempo noise segment, creating what we consider a truly epic ending. We also caught LILLIE CREATURES performing in Taipei once, and we knew we wanted to collaborate with her even before the album was finished. Although we didn’t deliberately tailor the writing to fit her style, the song naturally left space for her. Partnering with her was full of surprises, and we feel incredibly lucky to have her vocals on “Maru”. One of the most striking aspects of the record is the way repetition and transformation operate throughout the album. Pieces such as “Abyss I” and “Abyss II” mirror one another, while “Maru” and “Requiem” continually evolve through changes in instrumentation and texture. Were you consciously thinking in terms of narrative and world-building when composing these pieces, or did the sense of journey emerge naturally from the music itself? Halfway through the writing process (“Seven Steps,” “Mansion,” “Requiem” were finished), we mapped out a complete storyline for the entire album. Ultimately, the narrative and the music influenced each other reciprocally, shaping the final piece into what it is today. Acid Brain 酸腦 emerged from Taipei’s underground music scene with a strong DIY ethos, recording in bedrooms and rehearsal spaces and releasing music on your own terms despite the band’s young age. How would you describe the current underground scene in Taipei, particularly for heavier, experimental or psychedelic music? Do you feel that a new generation of Taiwanese artists is developing its own identity, and what role has that community played in shaping Acid Brain’s sound and outlook? There is a band in Taipei called Bremen Entertainment Inc. They are a heavy psychedelic band and our seniors, who won Album of the Year at our independent music awards. In their acceptance speech, they mentioned that their winning album was also recorded entirely in bedrooms and rehearsal spaces. We loved that idea. In this day and age, everyone should be able to produce the coolest records out of any underground setting with a low-cost approach. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items.body: Intelligent yet playful, We Thought It Was Normal is an assured statement from an artist continuing to refine an already distinctive electronic language. Technical precision with genuine warmth Augusta, Georgia’s Linear North expands an already impressive catalogue with We Thought It Was Normal, a self-released seven-track excursion through IDM, string-inflected house, and richly detailed sampledelia. Equal parts cinematic and rhythmically agile, the release balances technical precision with genuine warmth. “Echo Refuge” opens in contemplative fashion, its expansive atmosphere recalling early The Black Dog before “War Dog Flick” fractures into razor-sharp breakbeat manipulations, neo-funk syncopation, and playful edit work. It reinforces a simple truth: youthful exuberance remains a vital force in contemporary electronic music when guided by mature production instincts. Elsewhere, “Ghost Photo Metro” pairs intricate programming with emotive textures that suggest the human spirit lingering inside digital architecture, while “Brains Nor Backbone” echoes Plaid‘s gift for combining rhythmic sophistication with melodic openness. Every element feels purposeful, never excessive, allowing the compositions to breathe without sacrificing momentum. Closing piece “The Sacred Pattern” introduces an operatic vocal treatment that recalls the theatrical elegance of mid-period Kate Bush, adding an unexpected organic counterpoint to the album’s digital framework. Throughout, We Thought It Was Normal demonstrates that technical fluency needn’t come at the expense of accessibility. Intelligent yet playful, it is an assured statement from an artist continuing to refine an already distinctive electronic language. spaceShift is available on Bandcamp. items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — It is interesting how some people were lucky enough to experience the 70s and see those great bands when they were new, while others of us only learned the history later on; yet, regarding one of the most famous trios, the story is the same for everyone. Carl Palmer came from Atomic Rooster, Keith Emerson from The Nice, and Greg Lake from King Crimson. It was a supergroup with a history that preceded them, much like Cream, even though their music was very different.Keith Emerson's imprint, his classical influence and innovative adaptations (a signature style he had pioneered with The Nice), combined with a passion for jazz and improvisation, merged with the energy and precision of Carl Palmer. Palmer was a musical sponge, eager to learn and adapt his playing to the demands of the compositions, shifting his style as needed and cementing his legacy as one of the decade's greatest drummers. Then there was the lyricism of Greg Lake, possessor of one of progressive rock's finest voices and a superb bassist, who brought a fascinating, somewhat dark compositional edge from his time in Robert Fripp's band. All of this resulted in something extraordinary, something that took on a life of its own, spiraling beyond their control like a white dove released into the wild."The Barbarian," the album's opening track, is an adaptation of B�la Bart�k's Allegro Barbaro; right from the start, it showcased the group's contemporary edge, sounding modern, daring, and atonal. Keith Emerson demonstrated remarkable versatility and skill, equally adept at tackling classical scores, which he would interpret with wild abandon, and playing the blues on the Hammond organ. Greg Lake's distorted bass work was also a crucial element, helping to craft the dark, theatrical atmosphere of a spectacular debut."Take a Pebble" couldn't get off to a better start, featuring a texture so distinct and sophisticated that it feels like the beginning of a whole new album; Keith brushes the piano strings as if playing a harp, and the cascading piano notes herald one of the band's timeless tracks, a song where hearing the vocals is a delight rediscovered every time one revisits the record. The drum and piano passages respect the vocal phrasing until the instrumental section, driven by a highly fluid bassline, opens the door to jazz, allowing Emerson, Lake & Palmer to excel at what they did best: functioning as a jazz trio, playing at high speed with impeccable timing and groove, yet capable of switching to classical melodies at a moment's notice. After an acoustic passage featuring a rustic guitar style, an improvised section, part classical, part jazz, will follow, before the piece comes full circle to close with the same opening melody. And a finale... truly legendary, between Greg and Keith."Knife-Edge" also gets off to a great start following the end of the previous track; it is a rock song in the trio's signature style (complete with a J.S. Bach quote in the middle) featuring superb accompaniment from Carl Palmer."The Three Fates" begins with a Baroque-evoking pipe organ in "Clotho," the first movement. Then comes "Lachesis", the first of Keith Emerson's piano concertos, shifting from Baroque to jazz; when the drums join in, they create a marvelous pandemonium that breathed new life into music. With the third part, Atropos, reminiscent of Igor Stravinsky. There were excesses, certainly (criticized by many at the time) yet these are precisely what are best remembered and missed from that decade: the artistic excesses that drive history forward. "Tank", fueled by the drums, the inventive bassline, and Keith's furiously played clavinet, also makes for a perfect start following the piano concerto; the entire piece is flawlessly conceived as a cohesive whole. The clavinet improvises with a jazz-like sensibility, despite the classical sound, marking yet another innovation. It showcases the trio at the peak of their powers, including their compositional prowess; everything is meticulously crafted, for after that opening section, a Carl Palmer drum solo paves the way for a historic crescendo featuring Keith on the Mini-Moog.The foot seems to ease off the gas, and the album closes with a ballad that began as a very simple piece, instrumentally enriched by the trio, and has since become an anthem, forming part of the band's DNA in its less experimental guise. That didn't stop Keith from playing around with the Moog at the end of the track, however. Much like King Crimson, it was a stylistically mature debut, featuring an ambitious and rich musical vision that they would only go on to deepen over the course of that first five-year period.
